data.title: How a Small Potash Developer Jumped A Massive Hurdle in Saskatchewan
data.description:
Key points

  • Buffalo Potash has connected all three horizontal wells underground at its Disley Project in Saskatchewan, proving its patented extraction design works in practice.

  • By showing fluid can reliably move between wells, Buffalo has cleared the prime technical risk that kept it trading at a discount to conventional potash miners.

  • The next step is pumping potash-rich brine to the surface ahead of a targeted Q1 2027 production start, though the project is still advancing without a formal feasibility study.

If you look at the world’s major potash mines, almost all of them belong to the major players like Mosaic (NYSE:MOS) or K+S. That’s not coincidental. Extracting potash traditionally requires sinking vertical wells and billions of dollars in infrastructure. 

That expenditure is typically a barrier to entry that’s kept smaller players on the sidelines. 

Buffalo Potash (TSXV:BUFF) is trying to rewrite the playbook on a prime patch of land in the middle of Saskatchewan. A plot that happens to border Mosaic’s Belle Plaine mine and K+S’ Bethune operation. Instead of drilling straight down with expensive vertical wells, Buffalo opted to lay three 565-meter horizontal wells along the base of the deposit. Essentially, one central injector flanked by two producers. 

Until this week, that exact setup was one of the reasons investors were staying cautious. Using horizontal wells to dissolve potash underground is the new kid on the block. 

Buffalo patented it and dubbed it the “Horizontal Line-Drive” (HLD) method, which has never proven its mettle at this scale. Mostly due to the fact that if the salty water pumped down doesn’t reliably reach the outer wells, the whole model is kaput. 

Question quelled

That question was just answered. Following its first well connection on November 23, Buffalo confirmed on the 25th that it’s connected the second producer well, completing an underground loop across all three wells. They’ve also reported pressure and fluid readings matching the subsurface engineering model predictions.

“Connecting the second producer well gives us confidence that what we're seeing underground is repeatable, which is exactly what we set out to demonstrate at this stage," CEO Steve Halabura said, noting the team is now laser-focused on delivering brine to the surface. 

For the investors 

So, what happens next (and why does it matter)? Simply put, Buffalo has cleared the engineering hurdle that often snags other runners. From here on, the process relies on the same solution-mining principles used across the region for 60 years which is to circulate brine, dissolve the potash and pump the mineral-rich liquid up for processing. 

Before it sees sunlight however, engineers will use an 11-stage packer system. Sounds complicated, but it’s essentially just a series of adjustable internal seals along the wells that pressurize different sections and widen the flow underground. 

This is also known as the Mining Plane.

Disley: by the numbers

Quick note: Economic figures come from Buffalo’s May 2026 Preliminary Economic Assessment. All the details can be found in Buffalo’s November 25 release.

What it all means

For investors, the broader story is the proof in the method’s pudding and how the tech can potentially shift Buffalo’s valuation narrative seeing as horizontal solution mining is designed to deliver lower operating costs and a smaller environmental footprint. 

Successfully proving it works at the Initial Production Module (IPM) gives Buffalo a repeatable, low-CapEx blueprint to build on. 

Once the company hits first production, still targeted for Q1 2027, the IP will be proven for deployment across other spaces at Disley, which can handily lead to scaling to a 1.125 million-metric-ton-per-year target.

What could still go wrong?

There is still plenty of executional risk between an underground connection and commercial cash flow. Buffalo is advancing the starter plant based on assessments rather than formal mineral feasibility reports. This means the real-world recoveries, costs and timelines can still vary wildly. They’re also working to finalize a royalty deal with Altius Royalty Corporation (announced October 22) to fund the remaining site and surface processing build-out. 

This article was written independently by the author, without issuer input or approval. Buffalo Potash has a marketing services agreement with Simply Wall St. Details on compensation and other important information can be found in the disclosure and disclaimer at the end of this narrative.

Technical and scientific information in this article is drawn from Buffalo Potash Corp’s news release dated November 25, 2026, which was reviewed and approved by independent Qualified Person Jared Galenzoski, P.Geo., FIMMM, in accordance with National Instrument 43-101. Readers should note that no mineral reserves have been established at the Disley Project, the company’s decision to advance the Initial Production Module is based on a Preliminary Economic Assessment rather than a feasibility study, and its Horizontal Line-Drive mining method has not yet been operated at commercial scale.

data.title: Here's Why We're Not Too Worried About Neurogene's (NASDAQ:NGNE) Cash Burn Situation
data.description:
There's no doubt that money can be made by owning shares of unprofitable businesses. For example, although software-as-a-service business Salesforce.com lost money for years while it grew recurring revenue, if you held shares since 2005, you'd have done very well indeed. Having said that, unprofitable companies are risky because they could potentially burn through all their cash and become distressed.

So should Neurogene (NASDAQ:NGNE) shareholders be worried about its cash burn? For the purpose of this article, we'll define cash burn as the amount of cash the company is spending each year to fund its growth (also called its negative free cash flow). Let's start with an examination of the business' cash, relative to its cash burn.

AI is about to change healthcare. These 20 stocks are working on everything from early diagnostics to drug discovery. The best part - they are all under $10bn in marketcap - there is still time to get in early.

How Long Is Neurogene's Cash Runway?

A company's cash runway is the amount of time it would take to burn through its cash reserves at its current cash burn rate. When Neurogene last reported its September 2026 balance sheet in November 2026, it had zero debt and cash worth US$360m. Looking at the last year, the company burnt through US$98m. Therefore, from September 2026 it had 3.7 years of cash runway. Notably, however, analysts think that Neurogene will break even (at a free cash flow level) before then. If that happens, then the length of its cash runway, today, would become a moot point. The image below shows how its cash balance has been changing over the last few years.

Check out our latest analysis for Neurogene

How Is Neurogene's Cash Burn Changing Over Time?

Because Neurogene isn't currently generating revenue, we consider it an early-stage business. Nonetheless, we can still examine its cash burn trajectory as part of our assessment of its cash burn situation. With the cash burn rate up 24% in the last year, it seems that the company is ratcheting up investment in the business over time. That's not necessarily a bad thing, but investors should be mindful of the fact that will shorten the cash runway. While the past is always worth studying, it is the future that matters most of all. So you might want to take a peek at how much the company is expected to grow in the next few years.

Can Neurogene Raise More Cash Easily?

Given its cash burn trajectory, Neurogene shareholders may wish to consider how easily it could raise more cash, despite its solid cash runway. Issuing new shares, or taking on debt, are the most common ways for a listed company to raise more money for its business. One of the main advantages held by publicly listed companies is that they can sell shares to investors to raise cash and fund growth. By looking at a company's cash burn relative to its market capitalisation, we gain insight on how much shareholders would be diluted if the company needed to raise enough cash to cover another year's cash burn.

Since it has a market capitalisation of US$521m, Neurogene's US$98m in cash burn equates to about 19% of its market value. As a result, we'd venture that the company could raise more cash for growth without much trouble, albeit at the cost of some dilution.

So, Should We Worry About Neurogene's Cash Burn?

It may already be apparent to you that we're relatively comfortable with the way Neurogene is burning through its cash. For example, we think its cash runway suggests that the company is on a good path. While its increasing cash burn wasn't great, the other factors mentioned in this article more than make up for weakness on that measure. Shareholders can take heart from the fact that analysts are forecasting it will reach breakeven. Considering all the factors discussed in this article, we're not overly concerned about the company's cash burn, although we do think shareholders should keep an eye on how it develops. data.title: Just Four Days Till SLB N.V. (NYSE:SLB) Will Be Trading Ex-Dividend
data.description:
Some investors rely on dividends for growing their wealth, and if you're one of those dividend sleuths, you might be intrigued to know that SLB N.V. (NYSE:SLB) is about to go ex-dividend in just four days. The ex-dividend date is one business day before the record date, which is the cut-off date for shareholders to be present on the company's books to be eligible for a dividend payment. The ex-dividend date is of consequence because whenever a stock is bought or sold, the trade takes at least one business day to settle. Therefore, if you purchase SLB's shares on or after the 2nd of December, you won't be eligible to receive the dividend, when it is paid on the 7th of January.

The company's next dividend payment will be US$0.295 per share. Last year, in total, the company distributed US$1.18 to shareholders. Calculating the last year's worth of payments shows that SLB has a trailing yield of 2.4% on the current share price of US$48.52. If you buy this business for its dividend, you should have an idea of whether SLB's dividend is reliable and sustainable. That's why we should always check whether the dividend payments appear sustainable, and if the company is growing.

We've found 21 US stocks that are forecast to pay a dividend yield of over 6% next year. See the full list for free.

Dividends are typically paid from company earnings. If a company pays more in dividends than it earned in profit, then the dividend could be unsustainable. SLB paid out more than half (56%) of its earnings last year, which is a regular payout ratio for most companies. That said, even highly profitable companies sometimes might not generate enough cash to pay the dividend, which is why we should always check if the dividend is covered by cash flow. It distributed 45% of its free cash flow as dividends, a comfortable payout level for most companies.

It's encouraging to see that the dividend is covered by both profit and cash flow. This generally suggests the dividend is sustainable, as long as earnings don't drop precipitously.

Check out our latest analysis for SLB

Click here to see the company's payout ratio, plus analyst estimates of its future dividends.

Have Earnings And Dividends Been Growing?

Stocks in companies that generate sustainable earnings growth often make the best dividend prospects, as it is easier to lift the dividend when earnings are rising. Investors love dividends, so if earnings fall and the dividend is reduced, expect a stock to be sold off heavily at the same time. With that in mind, we're encouraged by the steady growth at SLB, with earnings per share up 7.2% on average over the last five years. Decent historical earnings per share growth suggests SLB has been effectively growing value for shareholders. However, it's now paying out more than half its earnings as dividends. Therefore it's unlikely that the company will be able to reinvest heavily in its business, which could presage slower growth in the future.

The main way most investors will assess a company's dividend prospects is by checking the historical rate of dividend growth. SLB's dividend payments per share have declined at 5.1% per year on average over the past 10 years, which is uninspiring. It's unusual to see earnings per share increasing at the same time as dividends per share have been in decline. We'd hope it's because the company is reinvesting heavily in its business, but it could also suggest business is lumpy.

To Sum It Up

Is SLB worth buying for its dividend? Earnings per share growth has been modest and SLB paid out over half of its profits and less than half of its free cash flow, although both payout ratios are within normal limits. In summary, while it has some positive characteristics, we're not inclined to race out and buy SLB today.

data.title: Why Silver Investors Are Paying Attention To What’s Happening At Alamos
data.description:
Key points

  • In October 2026, drilling intersected the high-grade Africa blind vein (669 g/t AgEq over 2.05 m), proving that unmined silver structures with zero surface indicators sit parallel to the 26 known veins at Alamos.

  • Unlike most early-stage explorers, Minaurum Silver (TSXV:MGG) already holds underground mining approval (MIA) in Mexico, which allows new discoveries to share existing infrastructure.

  • Through the rehabilitation of 600+ m of historic colonial tunnels and extending drill holes where warranted, management is compounding its resource scale ahead of a scheduled update without the buildout costs.

  • As a pre-revenue junior player (CA$78M-CA$91M market cap), Minaurum relies on equity markets to fund drilling and still must prove vein continuity.

Traditional silver investors typically see early-stage mining as a black box of technical jargon. But when we strip away the geology, the business logic looks more similar than you’d expect.

Take commercial real estate as an example. The best returns rarely come from buying unzoned land in the middle of nowhere (unless you’re a data center), they come from discovering untapped square footage on a property that’s already zoned, permitted and connected to the grid.

In mining, a “blind” vein is much the same. It’s a high-grade deposit of silver that never broke through to the earth’s surface, trampled over by surface prospectors for centuries who never suspected it was there.

For the uninitiated, “AgEq”, or silver equivalent, is the accounting shorthand used to evaluate secondary metals found in the same rock (gold, copper, lead etc) into a single, simple grade.

Silver’s demand

Silver is a hot commodity with a demand problem, used for solar panel, grid electrification and AI data center hardware manufacturing.

Finding projects with existing permits and near-term development paths is tough, especially while many junior exploration companies burn shareholder cash chasing unpermitted projects from scratch.

Enter Minaurum

On October 22, Vancouver-based Minaurum struck silver and demonstrated its sharp capital-allocation methodology at the Alamos Silver Project in Sonora, Mexico. A project it owns outright.

While drilling a known zone called “Europa Sur” during its 50,000 m Phase II expansion, company geologists spotted subtle changes in the surrounding rock continuing past their planned target depth.

Rather than shutting it down to save on drilling, the team kept going.

The hidden vein silver investors should know about

Roughly 50 m off to the side of their main target, Hole AL26-268 (for the non-miners: “AL” = Alamos, “26” = 2026 and “268” = the 268th hole drilled) intersected 2.05 m grading 669 g/t AgEq.

Composed of 270 g/t pure silver alongside gold, copper, lead and zinc credits, it follows Hole AL26-257, which cut 1.30 m of 592 g/t AgEq.

This newly named “Africa vein zone” lines up roughly 400 m away with a 2019 drill hole (AL19-018), leading to the hypothesis that a parallel deposit was hiding right next to the company’s existing footprint.

Asset and catalyst snapshot

  • Footprint

100%-owned, 37,928-hectare district with an initial resource of 55.2 Moz AgEq (320 g/t AgEq; 34.8 Moz pure silver) modeled across only 3 of 26 known vein zones.

  • The blind vein

The new Africa vein hit 2.05 m of 669 g/t AgEq and 1.30 m of 592 g/t AgEq ~50 m away from Europa Sur.

  • Broader hits

High-grade step-outs outside the initial resource at:

  • Europa Sur: 0.60 m of 1,140 g/t AgEq; 2.65 m of 367 g/t AgEq

  • Quintera: 1.50 m of 462 g/t AgEq

  • San Jose: 0.30 m of 782 g/t AgEq

  • Regulatory moat

Minaurum holds full MIA underground mining permits, the only recent production-permitted silver discovery in Mexico.

What the 17th-century miners left behind

Silver mining in Alamos dates back to 1683, underwriting centuries of colonial architecture until groundwater and the Mexican Revolution halted work around 1911.

Today, the historic Promontorio workings are where Minaurum has restored over 600 m of haulage tunnels. Geologists still walk past hand-chiseled stopes and a stone prayer altar carved into the wall from its initial discovery centuries ago.

Led by CEO Darrell Rader and VP of Exploration Stephen Maynard, Minaurum has turned that century-old footprint into a modern advantage.

Rather than proposing the traditional open-pit mine in a heritage town, the company designed an underground operation using the existing architecture. Which in turn earned community support and helped the firm secure full underground mining permits ahead of its expansion.

Why it matters for silver investors

Like any mining resource, silver wears a couple of hats: serving as a financial hedge and an industrial component. This dual role gives silver investments strong upside during supply squeezes, but can punish companies that burn cash on slow, dilutive builds.

Think back to the real estate analogy. True asymmetric upside comes from finding high-grade zones on already-permitted infrastructure, not paying for permits and construction costs twice.

Due to its proximity, the Africa vein could share future underground access and processing infrastructure for Minaurum, lowering capital intensity per ounce.

In this instance, there are three key signals that separate Minaurum from other speculative drillers:

  1. Permits

Core environmental and operating approvals, such as Mexico’s MIA permit, are secured before major expansion capital is used.

  1. Field agility

Technical teams have the resourcing and capability to extend holes when rock alteration warrants it, just as Minaurum did with Hole AL26-257.

  1. Multi-asset cushions

Gold, copper, lead and zinc credits help buffer margins when silver prices swing. Which it’s been known to do.

Operational risks and market realities

Despite the permit moat and drill momentum, commodities can always be volatile and Minaurum still carries the real-world risks of a pre-revenue junior developer including:

  • Equity dilution

It trades at around CA$0.19 to CA$0.22 per share throughout November 2026 and has a sub-CA$100M market cap. The firm generates no operating revenue and relies on equity markets to fund drilling and engineering.

  • Vein continuity risk

Narrow underground veins can pinch and swell necessitating tighter drill spacing to confirm mineable widths in the upcoming resource model.

  • Commodity and jurisdictional exposure

Economics remain sensitive to silver and base-metal price swings as well as regulatory consistency in Mexico.

As Minaurum folds the Africa blind vein into its updated resource estimate, the takeaway for investors is clear: when the silver market’s tight, the most valuable ounces are often hiding right beside infrastructure you already have permission to mine.

data.title: Is Malta Fab Expansion Altering The Investment Case For GlobalFoundries (GFS)?
data.description:
• GlobalFoundries joined U.S. and Japanese officials to break ground on a new 300mm fab in Malta, New York, under a U.S. Japan initiative that could add up to US$21b of funded capacity and materially expand output for automotive, industrial and connected infrastructure chips.
  • The firm is also deepening its robotics collaboration with Boston Dynamics, using Spot and testing the Atlas humanoid to support fab operations and workforce upskilling in AI and automation across sites in the U.S., Germany and Singapore.
  • Next, the focus shifts to how GlobalFoundries expanding, government backed Malta fabs could reshape the existing investment narrative and capacity story.
Spot fast movers reshaping AI manufacturing by scanning our curated list of 52 AI infrastructure stocks as you weigh what GlobalFoundries’ Malta and robotics push could signal for wider chip infrastructure.

GLOBALFOUNDRIES Investment Narrative Recap

To own GlobalFoundries, you need to believe the analyst consensus Narrative on Simply Wall St that higher value automotive, AI data center and communications demand will offset ongoing weakness in smart mobile devices and support the capital heavy buildout in silicon photonics, SiGe, FDX and power. The Malta expansion and Boston Dynamics partnership fit that operational story but do not change the near term swing factor, which is how quickly new capacity is filled on attractive terms.

The biggest current risk is still that elevated CapEx, recently around 23% of quarterly revenue, does not translate into sustained demand and pricing. This would pressure free cash flow and limit earnings power. The robotics rollout and workforce upskilling look incremental for short term numbers, so the main watchpoint remains utilization and mix in the newer AI and infrastructure lines.

The extended Boston Dynamics collaboration is arguably the most relevant news for near term execution. Wider Spot deployments across Malta, Burlington, Dresden and Singapore, plus early Atlas testing from 2027, speak directly to how GlobalFoundries is trying to run more complex fabs while capital intensity stays high and new lines such as silicon photonics and SiGe scale.

For catalysts, the interesting angle is operational rather than headline grabbing. If autonomous inspection and asset management help keep utilization in the high 80s% or better where demand exists, that supports the analyst consensus Narrative on Simply Wall St that capacity additions in communications infrastructure and AI related products can drive margin leverage. If integration is slow or costly, the risk is added complexity during an already demanding expansion phase.

GLOBALFOUNDRIES' current analyst storyline points to revenues of US$10.5b and earnings of US$1.8b by 2029, tied to a forecast 13.8% yearly revenue growth rate and an earnings increase of about US$1.6b from US$197.0m today.
